title: Can Mercedes stay ahead of their rivals at the Madring?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli continued his fine form in Madrid as he topped the times after Friday practice. But with a red flag causing disruption to everyone’s running, and very little long run data gathered on a brand-new track, it’s still all to play for heading into the weekend…

How good is Antonelli looking?

Pretty good, but that’s no surprise given the form he’s been in all season to be fair. The championship leader, who went from 19th to first at the last round in Italy, looked the more comfortable of the two Mercedes, with Antonelli able to quickly find a groove on the soft tyre in Free Practice 2.

Whether or not he can stay there remains to be seen, as the track is evolving quickly and is only set to get more rubbered in as the weekend progresses.

But given he’s in the best place on Friday, and that he and Mercedes tend to make good steps overnight into the weekend, he is in very good shape.

title: What the teams learned about the Madring after day 1 of running
excerpt:
Formula 1 drivers and teams finally had their first proper taste of the Madring in Friday practice, and it proved to be every bit as challenging as had been anticipated.

Simulation can only do so much, so there was a great deal for everyone to learn, and so many unknowns around set-up, power unit deployment, and tyre management. It was the last item that became a major talking point of the day, with tyre graining cropping up early in the first session.

Overall the verdict from the drivers on the new venue was positive.

“I actually really loved it,” said Pierre Gasly, who finished the day in P11. “It was very exciting. It's a track with a lot of adrenaline. At all the corners you kind of see the walls coming at you very quickly, and you’ve got to be extremely precise in your lines, how much you commit to the corner.

“It definitely has this type of like adrenaline element, which you don't always find, but usually find on a street track. So, pretty cool.

“A lot of high-speed, which is unusual for a street track, and it's kind of a mix between like Jeddah and Monaco all combined together. Always exciting to find a new track, and definitely very exciting driving-wise. Now, hopefully, in the race, we can still find opportunities to overtake.”

“I would say honestly it’s more difficult than some tracks,” said Oscar Piastri, who was P7 in FP2. “There's a lot of sections where you're not really brushing up against the walls, you're kind of turning or heading at them, and then you need to avoid them.

“So it makes things quite challenging. Definitely I think everyone is still getting up to speed. But when you get into a decent rhythm over one lap, it's pretty enjoyable. In race running, it's been a nightmare to try and manage the tyres with graining.

“So a lot of corners have been very difficult. It's been an interesting day. I think we are struggling a little bit for pace. But yeah, hopefully we can find a bit more tomorrow.”

Teams had anticipated that graining might be an issue, but the scale of it came as a shock to the system in FP1, which led to set-up tweaks for the second session.

Russell shares ‘the big question mark’ facing drivers in Madrid

“We thought it was a possibility,” said George Russell. “It's often a possibility on new tarmacs. The grip is very high, but you're sliding quite aggressively. With the deg we had in FP1, a six-stop race would have been the fastest way!

“FP2 was slightly better, and I'm sure the race on Sunday will be better again. But that's the biggest question mark.”

It was interesting to see most teams saving two sets of the C2 hard tyres – only Audi deployed them on Friday – which indicates that they will feature heavily in the race.

Inevitably teams had lots of work to do on setup given the need to find a compromise that works on a track that has so many different types of corners.

Ferrari looked competitive from the very start of FP1, although Team Principal Fred Vasseur cautioned that what matters is how the car behaves in Saturday’s Qualifying session.

“I think the good setup is the setup that will work in in quali, not in free practice,” he said. “We know that we'll have a huge track evolution even during the session. The most important is to anticipate the grip in Q3, and to be ready for Q3. It makes no sense to do the best in free practice, and not in quali.

“It's a challenge that you have approximately all the types of corners of the season, and it's a good exercise for the engineers. But at the end, it's also difficult to estimate what will be the grip evolution between FP3 and quali, and even during quali. It means that energy deployment is complicated with the high-speed section, and I think what will be key is to estimate the pace in Q3.”

While Ferrari looked good, with Charles Leclerc finishing FP2 in second place, Red Bull drivers Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were less satisfied with progress.

“I think it's better to not be happy during Friday!,” said Pierre Wache, echoing Vasseur’s suggestion that what matters is getting it right for the grip level come Qualifying.

“And there's a lot of work to do on car setup, for sure. Mechanical grip, I think the ride is more challenging than what we thought. It's not as smooth.

“On energy deployment, it's clear that we have a lot of work to do there also. And the tyres grained maybe as expected – I think in FP2 we were a little bit better than FP1, and I think we have to continue in this route.”

Wache agreed that it won’t be easy to get it just right: “I think compromising between corner and deployment, some corners are full throttle, and putting some sliding on the tyres. That's something we have to see. But yeah, it is a challenging one.”

And one of the biggest compromises is finding a set-up that works for the places where you have to jump kerbs and is effective throughout the rest of the track.

“It very difficult,” said Audi sporting director Inaki Rueda. “So the main set-up trade that we have here is between running low and stiff for aero, because you have lots of high-speed corners. And usually these cars, the more stiff and low you get the aero platform, the better it is.

“But you have the trade-off of jumping the kerbs, like jumping the kerb in Turn 2. It's a lot of lap time.

"We cannot not jump it, and of course for that you want a higher car, and more of a rolling car. And so that is where the trade-off is, and the answer is going to be difficult.”

title: F3: Kato and Taponen take pole in Madrid
excerpt:
Taito Kato took his maiden FIA Formula 3 pole position with a superb performance in Qualifying 1 in Madrid, while in Qualifying 2, it was Tuukka Taponen that came out on top.

In the battle for the championship, Ugo Ugochukwu was fourth in Q1 and second in Q2, while Freddie Slater was down in P17 in the opening session, and eighth in the second set of 20 minutes.

In Q1, Kato beat Rodin Motorsport’s Pedro Clerot to the top spot by just 0.012s with a 1:50.535.

Taponen was third ahead of Ugochukwu, while Enzo Deligny rounded out the top five.

With Saturday’s two Sprint Race grids set by the results of the first Qualifying session, PREMA Racing’s James Wharton will start from reverse pole position.

Campos’ Theophile Nael will line-up alongside him on the front row with the second PREMA of Alex Powell in third.

In Qualifying 2, Ugochukwu looked set for his first pole position in Formula 3 until Taponen eclipsed his time by 0.021s with a 1:49.750.

Clerot wound up P3 despite hitting the barrier at the final corner on his last lap. Kato was fourth, with Mattia Colnaghi in fifth.

That wraps up the day’s action with the Sprint Race set for 11:05 local time on Saturday morning. Until then, you can read a full report from today’s FIA Formula 3 Qualifying in Madrid on the official website here.

title: Madring Qualifying 'going to be an exciting one' – Leclerc
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes that Qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend is "going to be an exciting one", having got his first taste of the Madring on Friday.

Ferrari proved to be Mercedes' closest challenger during the opening day of practice at Formula 1's newest venue, which provided plenty of challenges for teams and drivers.

Leclerc finished P3 and P2 in the two, one-hour sessions and was just one-tenth behind Free Practice 2 pacesetter Kimi Antonelli after a positive day behind the wheel.

"It has been a very interesting day. Obviously it is a completely new track for everyone. It is a very, very challenging track and I think for Qualifying, it is going to be an exciting one," said Leclerc.

"Lots of work ahead of us to try and improve the car for tomorrow but I think the day went quite well. I think we went through our programme, which is important.

"We did maximise the amount of laps we could do which was also one of the main targets for today, being on a new track. Looking forward to tomorrow to try and do something good in Qualifying."

Leclerc has generally been strong on street circuits during his F1 career, but admits that he doesn't have a target in mind during Saturday's crucial Qualifying session, with overtaking likely to be difficult in Madrid.

"It is more about trying to maximise what we have and we will see at the end of Qualifying where that leaves us," he said.

"I expect the Mercedes is quite strong but you never know so I’ll just focus on myself, trying to optimise everything we can on our car and hopefully we can do something really good tomorrow."

Team mate Lewis Hamilton also showed strong pace, finishing P4 and P3, but Ferrari team boss Fred Vassuer is wary of the team's prospects so early into the weekend.

In particular, that the track's condition will only improve and move the goalposts that teams have calibrated to on Friday.

"I think we are far away of the lap time of Quali, the most important is to improve the competitiveness of the car and for the driver to understand the track also," said Vasseur.

"I think there is a lot of topic about energy deployment and so, that means racing is open and everybody will improve a lot. We just have to be focused on ourselves.

"I think we are all in the same boat, that track evolution is huge from one session to the other one, but almost from one lap to the other one balance is changing a little bit."

title: What the teams said – Friday in Spain
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on their initial impression of the Madring, after Friday practice for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Sep 11, 2026 6:32pm UTC

Mercedes

Mercedes got off to a good start in Madrid, with George Russell topping the session by a comfortable margin from his team mate. Kimi Antonelli did run wide at one point after locking up, though the pecking order remained a little unknown heading into FP2. Things became clearer in the second hour of practice, with Antonelli nailing his flying lap to top the leaderboard. The Italian looks quick, confident and happy to push which bodes well for the team, while Russell aborted his flying run and thus did not set a representative time.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:34.363, P2; FP2: 1:33.662, P1

"That is our first day done on track in Madrid and it is a very cool circuit to drive around. It is a real challenge for us as drivers, with lots of high-speed corners and walls close by. You need to be very precise with your lines and good on the brakes; it is very easy to lock-up as there are a lot of places where you are braking and turning at the same time. It is a fun challenge and one that I am enjoying.

"We’ve had a good first day here but there is still lots of work to do ahead of the rest of the weekend. It is going to be difficult to look after the tyres on Sunday and overtaking is likely going to be a real challenge. That makes our single lap work tomorrow morning even more important; we will focus on that overnight but also looking to ensure we have a good race car for Sunday."

George Russell - FP1: 1:34.077, P1; FP2: 1:33.999, P5

"It was very fun driving the Madring for the first time today. It is always an enjoyable experience when you get to try out a new track; this place is particularly challenging, which is good fun as we get to grips with it.

"We started well in FP1, and the car was strong from the off. We made some set-up changes for FP2 but I’m not sure they improved the car so we may row back on them overnight. The bigger question from today is the tyre degradation. It was very high in FP1 and, although it was reduced for FP2, the long Turn 12 really puts the tyres under pressure and that will be difficult to manage on Sunday. That is something we will need to be on top of if we are to be in the fight this weekend.

"We’re looking forward to the rest of the weekend now. Overtaking on the long run in FP2 was really tough so qualifying will be very important. We looked decent on the single lap but with the smoothness of the tarmac here, it wasn’t always straightforward to get the tyres working for lap one. That is something we will work on overnight and tomorrow in FP3; hopefully we can get ourselves in the battle for pole position."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"New circuits are always a good challenge for the engineers as the preparation work is so crucial to being able to hit the ground running. In that regard, we look to have done a solid job, and both drivers were improving steadily through FP1.

"The tyres were a bit tricky to get into the window but once we'd got them going, the grip was surprisingly high, and the drivers were able to set some decent times. It was good to see George top FP1 and Kimi top FP2 but the challenge with circuits like this is in keeping your car in the window as the track grip keeps evolving.

"Whilst we covered a lot of single lap work, the long run was cut short by the red flag in FP2. What we have seen though is that the front tyres are having a tough time and that is probably going to be the same story on Sunday. It looks tight at the front so we're going to have to find a bit more pace if we want to be in the battle for the front row tomorrow evening. Overall, the day has been encouraging though and it looks like we are as much in the fight as anyone else."

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Ferrari got the best start of the weekend, quickest on the medium tyres as their drivers traded fastest lap times. But once the softs went on, they struggled somewhat with both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc locking up. On top of that, Hamilton twice drew the ire of his fellow drivers, with both Nice Hulkenberg and Carlos Sainz complaining the Ferrari man was not getting out of the way. It was much of the same in FP2, both drivers looking quick and evenly matched, but both also struggling to keep the car on the racing line. If they can clean up their laps, they could be a match for Mercedes here.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:34.536, P3; FP2: 1:33.775, P2

"It was exciting to drive on the Madrid circuit today. It’s a challenging street track, which is the type I usually enjoy and this one is no exception.

"I was quite impressed with the amount of grip there already was, considering that this is a completely new track with not much rubber on it so far. Nevertheless, I expect the track evolution to be big over the course of the weekend.

"Our target was to maximise the number of laps and gather as much data as possible today, to get to know the track and prepare for qualifying, which will likely be the key moment of the weekend because overtaking is so difficult here. I look forward to seeing what we can bring home tomorrow."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:34.620, P4; FP2: 1:33.811, P3

"It’s a fun track to drive and FP1 was a good starting point for us. As the day went on, we found it a little more difficult to get the car in the right window, so there are a few things for us to look into, particularly around the balance. It’s a new circuit for everyone and we gathered plenty of useful data today, which we’ll go through overnight. There are definitely some positives to take and we’ll work to make a step forward ahead of qualifying tomorrow."

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

McLaren

It was a steady start for Norris in Madrid, but Piastri had more of a struggle with something coming loose in the footwell of his car. That sent the Australian back to the pits, and he was unable to come back out, missing crucial lap time. In the second session, it was the turn of Norris to lose running, the World Champion missing nearly the entire session with a gearbox issue. That leaves him majorly playing catch up tomorrow. Piastri did get plenty of laps in, and bar one moment at Turn 7, was solidly in the top 10 albeit not quite on the pace of Ferrari and Mercedes.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:34.947, P6; FP2: No time set, P22

"A tricky day, it was good to get the laps in this morning, where we identified a few changes we needed to make to the car, but ultimately we didn't get the chance to make any progress in FP2 due to a gearbox issue.

"Whenever you come to a new circuit, track time is very important, so we're clearly on the back foot having missed FP2. We'll work hard overnight looking at the data from FP1, from Oscar's car and the teams around us, and make sure we get as much learning as we can in FP3. Otherwise, it was good to get the first laps done here in Madrid, it's an interesting circuit and I'm looking forward to getting some more laps in ahead of Qualifying tomorrow.”

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:35.148, P8; FP2: 1:34.200, P7

"Overall, a solid day. Lots of learning and driving on a new track always makes things a bit tougher to get on top of. Once you settle into a rhythm it’s a pretty enjoyable one to drive but tyre management is going to be a tough one, as we have a lot of graining. I felt like we got a bit closer in FP2, which was a positive step, but we're still lacking pace, so we'll be working hard overnight to try and find more time.

"The main challenge is extracting the maximum performance from the car on a street circuit like this. Hopefully tomorrow we can find more consistency and unlock the ability to get that extra time out of the car. We’ll see what we can do.”

Mark Temple, Technical Director, Performance

"Today presented a significant challenge, particularly with the gearbox issue that cost Lando a substantial amount of track time in FP2. It's a big setback on a new and technically demanding circuit like this, where every lap is crucial for gathering data. The conditions are tough for everyone, with high temperatures and low grip, so losing that running time certainly puts us on the back foot heading into Saturday.

"Our focus tonight is on a deep dive into the data to see where we can unlock more performance. The car isn't quite where we want it to be, but we have some clear ideas on both the chassis and driver side to explore. We'll be working hard to analyse a wider variety of potential changes than usual to ensure we can give both drivers a more competitive package for Qualifying. Maximising Lando's track time in FP3 will be our absolute priority to help him recover.”

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes makes a pitstop during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: (EDITORS NOTE: Image has been digitally enhanced.) Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Pauline Ballet - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Red Bull

Both Mx Verstappen and Liam Lawson had clean opening sessions for Red Bull, with the former a solid fifth, and the New Zealander just sneaking into the top 10. It was much more of the same in FP2, Lawson again 10th although he did have to pit late on for the team to check his car over. Verstappen also had an issue, complaining about his steering, but other than that it was an okay but not spectacular opener for the team.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:34.703, P5; FP2: 1:34.063, P6

“Both sessions today weren’t too bad. We’re always trying to find extra pace and understand more about the tyres. It's all building confidence, especially here on a new track and I felt that we were getting up to speed lap after lap. There are always little things to tweak, work on and improve, and that’s what this evening is for. Tomorrow, we’ll look into the one-lap pace and how the tyres will perform on the long run but anything can happen, so let's hope it's a clean session and we get out of it what we need."

Liam Lawson - FP1: 1:35.539, P10; FP2: 1:34.938, P10

“For all of us, Madring is very different and takes a lot more time to get used to compared to tracks that we’ve been to many times over the years. The track is very exciting, it’s very fast in a lot of places, and very high commitment. FP1 was all about building up. The track gets a lot faster because it’s never really been driven on as we’re doing a lot of laps, putting rubber down, and making it faster, but I think after FP2, there’s definitely more time to find. I think the main goal for over the weekend is to try and do as many laps in Practice as possible and be prepared for Qualifying. So, we probably left a little bit of margin while getting used to the track, but everything feels okay so far. We’ll try and tune it up overnight and have a stronger drive tomorrow ahead of Qualifying."

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

“It was quite a smooth session, a normal Friday where you know you need to improve the car. In FP2 we were a little bit better than FP1. We did a lot of changes between sessions, and I think we will continue to explore some more changes ahead of FP3 as there's a lot of work to do on car set-up.

"Mechanical grip and the ride are more challenging than what we thought, the tyre grained more than expected, and the track is more bumpy than what we thought from the Sim, so there are some challenges. There’s a lot of different types of corners here so it’s interesting from an engineering point of view, but it looks like it’ll be difficult to overtake.

"We had some issues on Liam’s car at the end but managed to fix them. The long run was quite competitive, and our tyre management was quite good, so there’s some positives - but we know we’re not quick enough yet, so we have a lot of work to do."

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Liam Lawson of New Zealand driving the (30) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Yuki Tsunoda did not have the best openings to his weekend, with a power steering issue curtailing his running in FP1. He did not get a flying lap in on the softs and missed plenty of running as the team worked on his car. Arvid Lindblad did get a full session in and looked quick, although he was one of many left frustrated with traffic.

The rookie was fast in FP2 as well, before blotting his copybook when he lost the rear and crashed into the barriers, the first driver to bring out the red flags. That cut his session short, but he was able to walk away which was good to see. Tsunoda got a flying lap in during FP2, and wound up in the top 10 in an encouraging display.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:35.033, P7; FP2: 1:33.890, P4

"It was a positive first day for us here in Madrid. It didn’t feel like a completely new experience for me, as I’ve become quite used to learning a new track on a Friday this year. We showed good speed throughout the day and we were quick on every lap we completed in FP2. It wasn’t a nice feeling to end the session with a crash. It looked quite bad from the outside, but thankfully the impact wasn’t too heavy and I feel completely fine. There's some damage to the car, so I apologise to the team for the extra work they’ll have to do tonight. Finishing P4 on merit is a great result and puts us in a good position heading into tomorrow. I’ll focus on resetting tonight and taking the learnings from today for Qualifying."

Yuki Tsunoda - FP1: 1:36.939, P18; FP2: 1:34.758, P8

”It wasn’t the cleanest day today, but I’ve really enjoyed the new track which is super fun to drive. Confidence is key around here, so losing some track time in FP1 wasn’t ideal, plus I had a bit of traffic in FP2 which made things more difficult. Overall, I have a good feeling in the car. We’re building the pace session by session and now the focus is on pulling everything together for Qualifying tomorrow."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"If we look beyond Arvid's crash during FP2, it has been an excellent day for the team. The car is quick and the changes we made from FP1 to FP2 really improved the pace. The track here is also very impressive and it's clear a lot of time and effort has gone into creating an interesting circuit. We have a strong package as we head into Qualifying tomorrow and feel confident aiming for Q3 with both cars."

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Yuki Tsunoda of Japan driving the (22) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Haas

Esteban Ocon was the first driver to get on the radio and say the track was grippier than expected, with the Frenchman looking confident to push early on. He wound up an encouraging 12th, aero upgrades seemingly making a bigger difference here than they did last time out in Monza. Ollie Bearman took slightly longer to get going, and the same was true in FP2 – clipping the walls at one point.

Ocon was the happier of the duo, and wound up in the top 10 which bodes well for the team heading into Saturday, especially with grid slots set to be very important at this street track.

Esteban Ocon – FP1: 1:35.834, P12; FP2: 1:34.867, P9

“What’s positive is that we can have a feel of the new upgrades, much more than in Monza. There are a lot more corners, more grip-limited sections, and at the moment, we don’t have the inconsistency between cars, which is quite positive, so we need to have a good look at that. We’ll keep pushing, it’s been a very good day, so we need to keep at it. The track is extremely challenging in every aspect, but it’s very good fun, and I’m having a blast out there.”

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:36.853, P16; FP2: 1:35.203, P14

“It was an interesting first day at the Madring, it’s a cool track and it’s fun to drive – it feels to me like a hybrid of Baku and Jeddah. FP1 was a bit challenging, but we made a few changes on the car and made a big step forward for FP2, so I’m quite happy with the progress. Now I have the feeling in the car that I had in Monza, so I’m looking forward to seeing what we can do tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It was a decent Friday. It’s good that both cars are performing, because we had issues before and overall, when that happens, we can learn from both cars every single lap. We made good improvement between FP1 and FP2, where track conditions were good, although it’s a very challenging track. We tackled everything well, and tonight we need to look at tyre degradation, which everyone is suffering from – qualifying tomorrow is going to be very important. There’s some fine-tuning to do tonight in terms of tyre management and car balance, but it’s been a good start to the weekend.”

Esteban Ocon of France driving the (31) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Pauline Ballet - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain driving the (87) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari in the Pitlane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto was the only driver to run the hard compound tyre in FP1, with Audi splitting strategies between their cars. He finished 11th on the C2 rubber, which was a strong effort, a couple of places behind his team mate. Nico Hulkenberg did lock up at one stage, and was left very frustrated by Hamilton in terms of traffic. The team switched their drivers in FP2, with Hulkenberg running the hards and Bortoleto the mediums.

That leaves Audi as the only team with any experience of the C2 rubber heading into Saturday.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP1: 1:35.529, P9; FP2: 1:35.060, P12

"It was an interesting first day on a brand-new circuit. There was a lot to learn and plenty to explore, and it's definitely a unique track. It's incredibly fast, almost like a rollercoaster, with very little room for error, so it keeps you on your toes all the way around. We gathered plenty of information, and now it's about going through everything overnight, understanding what we've learned and seeing how we can use that to improve further."

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:35.652, P11; FP2: 1:35.170, P13

“It’s been great to finally get a first feeling of the Madring. Overall, it’s been a positive day for us: we learned a lot throughout the two sessions, although there is still some work to do overnight to try and extract some extra pace from our car. That will be our main task tomorrow – we’ll keep working, and I am looking forward to it.”

Alpine

Alpine sent Franco Colapinto out slightly late at the start of FP1, and then brought both cars back in so their early running was slightly compromised. Once they really got going, Colapinto was the pick of the two drivers. In the second session Pierre Gasly had the edge, but neither could make it into the top 10 with the circuit not seemingly suiting their car as much as Monza. But if they can hone those set-ups, there is no reason at least one car cannot sneak into Q3 tomorrow.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:36.473, P14; FP2: 1:34.959, P11

“It's always a nice challenge coming to a new circuit and seeing it at speed for the first time. I must say, I really loved the track. It's very exciting, it's high-speed and gives you a real adrenaline rush lap after lap. The walls come at you quite quickly, so you have to be very precise with lines and really commit to the corners throughout the whole lap. In terms of our day, I think it could have gone better and we have a few things we can improve. There is definitely more pace to find ahead of tomorrow, which should put us in the mix for the top ten.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:35.933, P13; FP2: 1:35.886, P15

“The Madring is certainly an exciting new track. We've spent a lot of time on the simulator preparing for it so to drive it for the first time for real today was very enjoyable. It's certainly an interesting track, very fast throughout and definitely one where you need everything to click into place. In terms of our day, Free Practice 1 was very much about learning the track and building things up step by step. As usual, in Free Practice 2, we did a bit of low fuel and high fuel to give us some ideas and data to learn from going into the rest of the weekend. We need to find some improvements and now we'll put some time in with the team and the engineers to find which direction on set-up to go.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“It was a day of learning and acclimatising to a new track and getting laps under our belt and going through the data. Of course, the drivers have spent a lot of time on the simulator, but there's nothing better than the real thing. There can be subtle differences on a new track, where the bumps are and how the car reacts or handles is important to get used to. It's a modern track with character and unique elements that make it exciting, which drivers have certainly expressed they enjoy. It's a test for the drivers and finding the limit here will reward lap time, so that's why there's been some stoppages today. We knew coming here this track would be different to last week and doesn't play to the strengths of our package like in Monza. We need to look at the data and make improvements to the car, as both drivers have similar feedback on drivability and some limitations on ride and traction.”

Williams

Williams suffered higher than expected degradation in the first session, with both the front-left and rear-left proving problematic and limiting what they could do in terms of lap time. Home favourite Carlos Sainz was the pick of the two drivers, although he cut a frustrated figure when he lost a flying lap time to traffic.

It was much of the same for the team in FP2, with Sainz again the pick of the duo as the Spaniard did his best to give the home crowds something to cheer.

Alex Albon - FP1: 1:37.591, P20; FP2: 1:36.936, P18

“It was challenging out there today; there are a lot of different style corners, so it was quite tough on the tyres. I also struggled with deployment as it felt quite different lap to lap, so I just felt like I never fully found a rhythm with the car. The SIM correlation wasn’t too far off, so that’s a positive, but we’ve got a fair bit of work to do as a team. I thought it was going to be a bit more of a qualifying weekend, but I think with the extra-long pit lane, race pace and strategy are going to be factors we need to consider.”

Carlos Sainz - FP1: 1:36.870, P17; FP2: 1:36.291, P16

“Friday done in Madrid! We've had a relatively smooth day with no issues or incidents, just a good couple of sessions where we could experiment with the setup. The track is spectacular. It's one of those tracks that gets you going when you're in the car, and it feels hectic to say the least, but I'm really enjoying it. Unfortunately, we don’t seem competitive at this circuit, but we'll do the best we can to put together a strong weekend and see what we're able to do.”

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso sounded like he was looking forward to his second home race of the season, and he had fun out there, pushing the boundaries and winding up a credible P15 with a late flying lap. But he suffered a clutch issue when completing the practice starts at the end of the session, and that meant he missed the start of FP2 as his car was repaired.

He did manage to get out though, but gave a sarcastic thumbs up when his flying lap on the softs was wrecked by traffic. He did beat his team mate, Lance Stroll struggling for pace out there.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:36.473, P15; FP2: 1:36.780, P17

Lance Stroll - FP1: 1:37.254, P19; FP2: 1:37.273, P20

Fernando Alonso says:

"It was about getting familiar with the new track today and working on some optimisation of the car setup.

"Unfortunately, we had an issue with the clutch at the end of FP1 and that left us with a slightly delayed start to FP2.

"It's going to be tricky to get it right tomorrow in Qualifying with the traffic and battery management, but we'll look to execute everything as best we can."

Pedro de la Rosa, Team Ambassador says:

"It's been an interesting first day at the Madring.

"It's a great track – challenging for both the drivers and the teams – and we collected a lot of data, which is positive.

"However, Fernando had a clutch issue at the end of FP1, which compromised the start of FP2 as he missed around 20 minutes, but the team in the garage did a great job to resolve it and minimise the time lost. That left Fernando slightly out of sync, running the Medium and Soft tyres when everyone else was doing high-fuel running, so he encountered some traffic on his final lap.

"Lance was going through the programme very well before suffering a suspected battery issue, which brought his FP2 session to a slightly early end.

"We would have liked to give both drivers more laps because, on a new street track, the more laps you do, the more confident you become when pushing to the limit, but there are still plenty of good learnings to take from today."

Cadillac

Cadillac had a clean opening hour of practice, with both drivers managing plenty of laps out there. Sergio Perez shaded his team mate, with their eyes firmly set on trying to battle with Aston Martin and Williams this weekend. The Mexican was again the faster of the two in the second session, as Valtteri Bottas struggled more with rear grip out there.

Valtteri Bottas - FP1: 1:38.818, P22; FP1: FP2: 1:37.727, P21

“A productive first day at the Madring. A new circuit for everyone and we are constantly learning. It’s unique with its tight and flowing sections which provides a good challenge. We completed two good sessions today, but we still have a lot of work to do in order to get the balance right and get the most out of the tyres. Overall though, a good first step and I look forward to debriefing so we can analyse the data with the engineers tonight.”

Sergio Perez - FP1: 1:38.150, P21; FP2: 1:37.195, P19

“It's a really cool track and a great venue. I’m so happy to be racing in Madrid and I'm confident this is going to become one of the best races in Europe. We have some work to do with the setup of the car overnight, but it was a good day overall and we were able to get some valuable data on long running.”

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Sergio Perez of Mexico driving the (11) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 11: Valtteri Bottas of Finland driving the (77) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 11, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

"Today was particularly important as it allowed both us and the teams to gather the first real-world data from a completely new circuit. Unfortunately, the red flag in the middle phase of the second free practice session reduced both the number and length of the long runs, limiting the amount of information available from a race perspective. We observed graining on both the front and rear left tyres, in some cases quite significant, which contributed to accelerating wear on the cars most prone to sliding. Differences between the teams are already becoming apparent in terms of who is able to manage the tyres more effectively over a stint.

"Track conditions were very good from the outset, with grip levels among the highest seen so far this season. The combination of high grip and a very smooth track surface encouraged the onset of graining, although this should ease slightly as the circuit continues to evolve, a trend that was already noticeable throughout the day. The Hard tyre represents the most important option for the race, given degradation levels higher than initially expected and the high temperatures that are forecast to persist over the coming days. The performance gap between the Medium and Soft compounds proved smaller than anticipated, averaging around half a second.

"Looking ahead to tomorrow’s qualifying session, it will be crucial to maximise the first flying lap in order to avoid the onset of thermal degradation, while carefully managing traffic, which could prove to be a decisive factor around this circuit."

title: Oliver Bearman spots 'oversight' in new Madrid F1 track layout
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman has spotted what he believes to be an "oversight" in the track design for the new Spanish Grand Prix venue in Madrid.

The Madring becomes the 79th circuit to host a world championship grand prix this weekend with the new 22-turn 3.3-mile layout around the IFEMA entertainment complex near to the Real Madrid training centre.

The semi-permanent street track is expected to be a major challenge, with Turn 12 in particular, La Monumental, a huge banked right-hander in the middle of the lap.

Overtaking is expected to be a challenge, with the high number of 90-degree 'point and squirt' corners, especially in the second-half of the lap, with overtaking set to be difficult with so few opportunities.

One such place is into Turn 5, at the end of the first SM-mode straight, but as Haas driver Bearman has pointed out, the braking zone into the left-right-left chicane that follows is curved - thus limiting chances for a move to be successfully made.

"It seems to be a track where it's going to be a big challenge to overtake, and it is a shame in a way because I think the layout is okay," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365.

"But there are some features of the circuit which naturally deter overtaking. One of them is the braking for Turn 5, which is curved, and that's the real overtaking opportunity, and that curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and sending one up the inside.

"So that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight, but it means that we're going to be fully focused on qualifying, and to do a good qualifying, of course, you need full confidence, and that starts from your first lap on Friday.

"I think it's going to be one of those races where we're very much focused on qualifying, similar to Budapest, Monaco, or even Zandvoort.

"In the simulator, you don't drive around with the fear of hurting yourself or the car, so the goal of the sim is to try and hit every wall possible in a way, because like that you learn exactly where the limits are and you find them in the most efficient way possible, and by doing that, you don't do that on the real track.

"It's definitely a tough track. But every street track I go to on the sim, it's pretty normal that you're bouncing off the walls quite a lot because that's the beauty of the simulator."

title: Madring reveals staggering difference between Mercedes, Ferrari and the rest
excerpt:
The first two free practice sessions at the new Madring track immediately painted a striking picture as Mercedes and Ferrari appear to be the only teams to have found the optimal balance in their cars.

The first two free practice sessions at Madring immediately made it clear that only two teams, Mercedes and Ferrari, were able to find the optimal balance in their cars right from the first free practice session.

In the second session, both teams confirmed this trend and were able to further refine their performance between the two practice outings.

This is an important observation, as it shows that the W17 and SF-26 appear to be the only 2026 F1 cars that are truly well-rounded.

They are therefore capable of being competitive on various types of circuits and thus demonstrate less track-specificity than their rivals.

Although both cars base their performance on different strengths, the W17 still holds an advantage in terms of powertrain performance.

Ferrari, on the other hand, demonstrates excellent vehicle dynamics, thanks to the car’s responsiveness during rapid direction changes in the second sector of the track.

© XPBimages

Mercedes, Ferrari carry out minimal changes

Like all other teams, Mercedes and Ferrari had to base their setup exclusively on predictive data, as no actual data was available beforehand.

As a result, it quickly became obvious that the dynamic responses of both cars to the chosen setups formed the foundation upon which the engineers could build during the two sessions to gradually improve performance further.

This became even clearer when we look at the differences between the teams in the second session, which had narrowed to just one-tenth of a second.

As grip on the track increased, both teams were able to further optimise their setups without completely overhauling them.

Compared to the morning, only minimal changes to the setup were necessary.

Tyre performance now the deciding factor

As mentioned, the strengths on which both cars base their performance differ.

On this track, however, there is no clear dominance of either concept in the various sectors.

The technical section of the circuit is just as important as the high-speed section. A setup focused entirely on one of these two aspects would therefore be a mistake.

It’s all about finding a compromise between downforce and efficiency. The battle now hinges primarily on tyre performance.

Tread wear appeared quite evident on all cars. However, despite the harsh conditions - particularly the very high track temperatures - Mercedes and Ferrari were able to maintain a fairly consistent pace during the long runs.

In short, so far it appears that there won’t be a third team in Spain capable of joining the battle between Mercedes and Ferrari.

title: The sheer bravery behind F1's greatest drive - 50 years on
excerpt:
September 12th marks half-a-century since the greatest single drive in the history of the F1 world championship.

12 September 9:00AM

As of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, there have been 1,162 world championship F1 races, competed in by 782 drivers.

357 of those have scored a point, 116 have won at least one grand prix, just 35 of them have become world champion, and even fewer- perhaps only a handful have become true household names.

There have been iconic rivalries, iconic cars, and moments of sporting skill and brilliance akin equal to anything in any major sport, but what is the best single performance in a race from a driver?

Perhaps it might be Max Verstappen at the awfully wet 2024 Sao Paulo GP where, from 17th on the grid, he firmly put Lando Norris in his place and swatted away any lingering title hopes for the McLaren driver. Maybe, its Lewis Hamilton at the 2008 British Grand Prix, where in typically Silverstone conditions, he lapped the field up to third place and won by 66 seconds?

How about Michael Schumacher winning the 2000 Japanese GP to finally end the wait for Ferrari after 21 years of waiting for a championship? Then there's Jackie Stewart's virtuoso performance at the 1968 German GP at the Nurburgring, where in terrible conditions and with his wrist in a cast, he won at the track he would dub 'The Green Hell' by over four minutes.

But then what about Juan Manuel Fangio putting Peter Collins and Mike Hawthorn in his shadow with the storming victory at the 'ring in 1957, where a botched pit-stop cost the great Argentine buckets of time, but roaring past to capture his fifth and final world championship?

Incredible drives all, and they all rightly feature in the top 10 of the greatest drives in F1 history. They all share in common that they were race victories, something you might regard as a perquisite for the honour of 'greatest drive in F1 history.'

But you would be mistaken.

For the single greatest drive in F1 history did not result in a victory, nor even in a podium finish. It was a 'mere' fourth place, and it came, on this day, September 12th, 50 years ago, at the 1976 Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

The driver? Niki Lauda.

© XPBimages

Lauda drive is the greatest in F1

The seeds for Lauda's performance at the 1976 Italian GP came just six weeks earlier after his famous crash at the Nurburgring in the German GP on August 1st.

That story is well-known. The reigning world champion was administered the last rites twice and suffered damage to his lungs due to the hot and toxic gases he inhaled after his helmet had been wrenched off in the impact. He even slipped into a coma.

He decided to limit the amount of reconstructive surgery, focusing mainly on his eyelids to restore their functionality.

The expectation was that Lauda would be out for the rest of the 1976 season at a minimum, and would return to mount a bid to reclaim his crown in 1977 after healing and recovering.

He missed the Austrian and Dutch Grands Prix, but stunningly, he announced he was returning for the Italian Grand Prix - just 42 days after he had cheated death.

Ferrari had been caught so on the hop by Lauda's Lazarus impression that it had to run three cars after Carlos Reutemann had been drafted in to partner Clay Regazzoni as the Austrian's temporary replacement.

Lauda qualified fifth for the race, with title rival James Hunt down in 27th on the 29 car grid, after his best time was disallowed for apparent 'fuel irregularities.' This meant that officially, the Briton had not qualified for the 26-car grid, but after the driver in 26th, Otto Stuppacher, had already left the track to head home, Hunt was allowed back in. The allegations of fuel irregularities were later withdrawn.

In the race, Ronnie Peterson won for March, with Regazzoni second, and Jacques Laffite third for Ligier ahead of Lauda in an unremarkable and quiet fourth place.

After the race, in which he later admitted he was "petrified", Lauda removed his helmet to reveal the blood-soaked balaclava which had stuck to his still raw and weeping wounds.

It was the ultimate performance, testing the bounds of human endurance as far as they could possibly go, all in the name of the pursuit of a few world championship points.

His wounds were still so raw that, if this had happened today, the decision would have been taken out of Lauda's hands by the medical advice. He was, in any era, in any medical advice, decidedly unfit to return to the cockpit of a racing car just six weeks after nearly paying the ultimate sacrifice.

Lauda's act of pure defiance in racing at Monza that day stands as the greatest act of bravery in sporting history. Not just motorsport, but in any sport by any athlete, male or female, successful or not.

It stands alone, and is unlikely ever to be beaten. It is hard to imagine in which circumstances an athlete could ever be allowed to compete in such a physical condition as Lauda was in that day. Modern medicine would simply not permit it.

title: George Russell hints at drastic Mercedes overhaul at Spanish GP
excerpt:
It was a strong day for Mercedes as the Spanish Grand Prix kicked off, but there may be work on George Russell's side of the garage.

George Russell has hinted that he may "row back" on set-up changes Mercedes made to his F1 car on Friday at the Spanish GP.

Russell topped FP1 in Madrid, but fell to fifth fastest in FP2 as team-mate Kimi Antonelli topped the times, as Russell aborted his first flying lap on the soft tyres during the qualifying simulation runs.

After a front-wing flap adjust, Russell then set the fifth-quickest time on his second lap on that set of soft tyres.

Another factor teams must take into account at the Madring is high levels of tyre graining, with Russell feeling that if the team "are in the fight" it needed to be on top of the tyres, especially through Turn 12 - La Monumental.

"We started well in FP1, and the car was strong from the off. We made some set-up changes for FP2 but I’m not sure they improved the car so we may row back on them overnight," he said.

"The bigger question from today is the tyre degradation. It was very high in FP1 and, although it was reduced for FP2, the long Turn 12 really puts the tyres under pressure and that will be difficult to manage on Sunday.

"That is something we will need to be on top of if we are to be in the fight this weekend.

"We’re looking forward to the rest of the weekend now. Overtaking on the long run in FP2 was really tough so qualifying will be very important.

"We looked decent on the single lap, but with the smoothness of the tarmac here, it wasn’t always straightforward to get the tyres working for lap one.

"That is something we will work on overnight and in FP3; hopefully we can get ourselves in the battle for pole position."

The article continues below.

© XPBimages

Antonelli sets the pace in FP2 in Spain

After topping FP2 at the new Spanish GP host venue from the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, Antonelli spoke of the technical challenge of the circuit, and how nailing single-lap pace was going to be crucial.

"It is a very cool circuit to drive around. It is a real challenge for us as drivers, with lots of high-speed corners and walls close by," he said.

"You need to be very precise with your lines and good on the brakes; it is very easy to lock-up as there are a lot of places where you are braking and turning at the same time. It is a fun challenge and one that I am enjoying.

"We had a good first day here, but there is still lots of work to do ahead of the rest of the weekend. It is going to be difficult to look after the tyres on Sunday and overtaking is likely going to be a real challenge.

"That makes our single lap work on Saturday morning even more important; we will focus on that overnight, but also look to ensure we have a good race car for Sunday."

title: Lando Norris to rely on Oscar Piastri information in Madrid 'backfoot' recovery
excerpt:
Lando Norris missed out the entire FP2 session at the Spanish Grand Prix and will be forced to play catch-up.

12 September 7:20AM

Lando Norris has explained how he will be relying on Oscar Piastri's data to aid his understanding after losing his second practice session at the Spanish GP.

Early in FP2 at the Madring, Norris pulled into the pits and reported that the gearbox on his MCL40 machine had gone into a "false neutral" and that it was "gone."

McLaren attempted to change the gearbox during the session, but eventually ran out of time, meaning Norris has lost one-third of his three hours of practice at the new circuit.

Meanwhile, Piastri completed 24 laps in FP2 to place seventh, with the world champion explaining how he would be relying on the Australian's data to aid his own understanding.

"A tricky day, it was good to get the laps in during the morning, where we identified a few changes we needed to make to the car, but ultimately we didn't get the chance to make any progress in FP2 due to a gearbox issue," Norris said.

"Whenever you come to a new circuit, track time is very important, so we're clearly on the back foot having missed FP2.

"We'll work hard overnight looking at the data from FP1, from Oscar's car and the teams around us, and make sure we get as much learning as we can in FP3.

"Otherwise, it was good to get the first laps done here in Madrid; it's an interesting circuit, and I'm looking forward to getting some more laps in ahead of qualifying."

The article continues below.

© XPBimages

Piastri's early warning

As for Piastri, he felt that it was initially tricky to master the Madring, but that a rhythm was possible, although he warned of tyre graining as a potential factor during the race.

"I felt like we got a bit closer in FP2, which was a positive step, but we're still lacking pace, so we'll be working hard to try and find more time.

"The main challenge is extracting the maximum performance from the car on a street circuit like this.

"Hopefully we can find more consistency and unlock the ability to get that extra time out of the car. We’ll see what we can do."

title: Lewis Hamilton names fresh target as Ferrari undergo tough Madring 'exercise'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was optimistic at where Ferrari stand following Friday practice at the Spanish GP, but is targetted a specific boost.

Lewis Hamilton is targetting improvements to the balance of his Ferrari at the Spanish Grand Prix, as boss Fred Vasseur spoke of the "good exercise" the engineers were experiencing.

Hamilton finished fourth and third, respectively in the two practice sessions on Friday at the Madring, and was just over a tenth slower than FP2 pace-setter Kimi Antonelli.

With the tight 90-degree point and squirt corners and the chicanes, the Madring is a layout tipped towards the strengths of the Ferrari, with Hamilton believing the team had a strong "starting point" but wants improvements heading into FP3 and qualifying.

One such was how the car seemed to get "more difficult" as the day progressed, with qualifying due to take place 24 hours after FP2.

"It’s a fun track to drive, and FP1 was a good starting point for us," Hamilton explained.

"As the day went on, we found it a little more difficult to get the car in the right window, so there are a few things for us to look into, particularly around the balance.

"It’s a new circuit for everyone and we gathered plenty of useful data, which we’ll go through.

"There are definitely some positives to take, and we’ll work to make a step forward ahead of qualifying."

The article continues below.

Ferrari set for "good exercise"

His Ferrari boss Vasseur then spoke of the "good exercise" the engineers are having in trying to simulate the best energy management for the lap, given the track evolution is expected to be huge, even through qualifying.

"I think the good setup is the setup that will work in qualifying, not in free practice," said Vasseur.

"We know that we'll have a huge track evolution even during the session. The most important thing is to anticipate the grip in Q3 and to be ready for Q3. It makes no sense to be the best in free practice and not in qualifying.

"It's a challenge as you approximately have all the types of corners of the season, and it's a good exercise for the engineers.

"But at the end, it's also difficult to estimate what the grip evolution will be between FP3 and qualifying, and even during qualifying, that means that energy deployment is complicated with the high-speed section, and I think that's what will be key is to estimate the pace in Q3."

title: Max Verstappen uses Liam Lawson example to point to wider F1 issue
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has highlighted Liam Lawson's rapid adaptability to the Red Bull challenger as further criticism of the current F1 regulations.

Lawson was called up to stand in for Isack Hadjar at the Dutch Grand Prix last month and retained the seat at Monza and Madrid as the Frenchman heals an injured wrist.

Yuki Tsunoda was called back to the sport to replace Lawson at Racing Bulls, and ended the Italian Grand Prix inside the points.

Verstappen has long voiced his concerns with the new-for-2026 cars and how unnatural the drivers are having to approach them to extract performance.

Reiterating his stance to BBC Sport, Verstappen said: "In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner.

"But now you're constantly thinking about, 'In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.'

“Stuff like that. It's so unnatural. It's so not how it should be.”

Many drivers have noted on occasion this year that they do not feel completely in control when it comes to extracting speed, with the battery doing a lot of the work on the straights.

Verstappen pointed to how quickly Lawson and Tsunoda got up to speed in their new cars as a clear example of a shortcoming with the current challengers.

"No disrespect, I hope no-one picks up on this, but look at Yuki [Tsunoda]," he said. "He jumps in the [Racing Bulls] car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

"Liam [Lawson] jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull - immediately competitive. It's because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

"Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit.

“The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it's really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You're held back."

title: Max Verstappen pinpoints two critical factors for Red Bull improvement
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has circled two key areas he wants to see improvement in from Red Bull overnight after a solid if unexceptional first day of the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

Max Verstappen identified one-lap pace and long-run tyre understanding as the two key areas Red Bull must address after finishing fifth in FP1 and sixth in FP2 on the opening day of the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion ended FP2 four-tenths adrift of session-topping Kimi Antonelli, having earlier trailed George Russell by six tenths of a second in FP1 as Mercedes dominated proceedings on the new Madrid circuit.

It was far from a disastrous day, but equally not a straightforward one. Verstappen was heard over team radio during the sessions complaining that the RB22 felt "loose" on corner exits while battling "weird understeer" through the middle of corners, telling the team at one point: "Car is still loose… I need the other wing," as Red Bull trialled different rear wing configurations throughout the day.

Despite the radio frustrations, Verstappen was measured in his assessment afterwards, zeroing in on two specific areas where gains must be found ahead of qualifying.

"Yeah, not too bad, just trying to find a little bit more pace over one lap, trying to understand the tyres a little bit more in the long run, and then just getting properly up to speed a bit more lap after lap," Verstappen said after FP2.

For Verstappen, the priority is clear, and Friday's running left the 71-time grand prix winner wanting more from the car's balance across all corner types and tyre compounds.

"Everything was okay," he added. "There are always little things in a practice session that you want to work on, improve on. So that's what we'll try to do for tomorrow, and then we'll see where we end up.

title: McLaren name 'absolute' Lando Norris priority after 'significant' setback
excerpt:
McLaren has named ensuring Lando Norris gets the maximum possible track time in FP3 at the Spanish Grand Prix as its "absolute priority."

Norris missed all of FP2 at the Madring - aside from two slow laps - with a gearbox issue, reporting that the process of losing it, the 'box had gone into 'false neutral.'

It means the world champion has lost one-third of the total practice time available at the new Spanish GP venue, and will be on the backfoot heading into FP3, where he must condense his qualifying simulations and race pace runs into the sole hour remaining.

Reflecting on the tough day, McLaren's engineering technical director, performance, Mark Temple explained that the team's priority was to ensure Norris maximised that sole remaining hour as it also worked through a "deep dive" to put the MCL40 into a competitive performance window.

"Today presented a significant challenge, particularly with the gearbox issue that cost Lando a substantial amount of track time in FP2," Temple explained.

"It's a big setback on a new and technically demanding circuit like this, where every lap is crucial for gathering data. The conditions are tough for everyone, with high temperatures and low grip, so losing that running time certainly puts us on the back foot heading into Saturday.

"Our focus tonight is on a deep dive into the data to see where we can unlock more performance. The car isn't quite where we want it to be, but we have some clear ideas on both the chassis and driver side to explore.

"We'll be working hard to analyse a wider variety of potential changes than usual to ensure we can give both drivers a more competitive package for qualifying. Maximising Lando's track time in FP3 will be our absolute priority to help him recover."

title: Fernando Alonso reveals 'near impossible' task at new Spanish GP circuit
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has explained he faces a task he has described as "nearly impossible" in his attempt to salvage a crumb of home comfort this weekend.

On the opening day of the Spanish Grand Prix weekend at the new Madring circuit in Madrid, Alonso's FP2, in particular, was badly compromised by a clutch issue with his Aston Martin at the start of second practice he suffered following his practice starts at the end of FP1.

As Alonso noted, the lack of early running in that session put him "out of sync", and "a little bit behind the programme", completing just 16 laps in contrast to a number of drivers who posted lap totals in the mid-20s.

Alonso eventually finished 17th quickest, offering a glimmer of hope he may qualify in Q2, albeit aided by the fact that McLaren's Lando Norris failed to post a time due to his MCL60 encountering a gearbox problem which required a change.

Assessing what might be possible going into the race, the two-time F1 champion does not doubt that the imposing 22 corners of the Madring will mean "it's going to be hard to overtake".

As for himself in the AMR26, he said: "For us, nearly impossible with the deficit on the straight, so qualifying will be important.

"At the same time, with the walls that close, the possibilities of a safety car or red flags, all these kinds of things, we need to stay focused. We need to see the chequered flag, do our own race.

"Whatever is the result in qualifying, I think there's still hope for Sunday, if we do a perfect execution of the race."

[Article continues below]

Alonso calls for 'fix' on 'a couple of things

Surprisingly, despite the pre-event suggestion there would be numerous incidents in the lead-up to the weekend given the tricky nature of the track, there was only one red flag across the two hours of practice running.

That was sparked by Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad 35 minutes into FP2 as he lost control of the rear of his car through the fast Turn 13 left-hander.

Traffic was also a problem, as Alonso discovered, and whilst he is confident of an improvement in qualifying, there are ongoing issues with the Honda power unit that will not aid his cause.

"It was tricky out there with the traffic, but it was our mistake to be out of sync," said Alonso. "Tomorrow in quali should be better.
